title: FinTech Wales Meets Economy Minister on Capital, Talent and Growth
snippet: Industry leaders and Cabinet Minister Adam Price discussed funding access, skills gaps and how Welsh fintechs can scale internationally. The post FinTech Wales Meets Economy Minister on Capital, Talent and Growth appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
FinTech Wales convened a roundtable with Adam Price MS, Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy, on 1 October, bringing together leaders from across Wales’ fintech and financial services sector to address three structural constraints: access to capital, talent pipelines and international growth.

Companies represented at the event, hosted at Tŷ Admiral in Cardiff, included Admiral, Hodge Bank, Principality, Vodafone Business, Collections Cloud, IE Hub, Driverly and several other Welsh fintech and financial services firms. The session was framed as a direct exchange between industry and government, rather than a formal consultation, with the intent of surfacing actionable commitments.

Capital and culture

A recurring theme was Wales’ risk-averse investment culture, which several attendees said was limiting the ambition of early-stage companies. One participant called for a regulatory or policy sandbox that would give companies room to develop genuinely innovative products without facing disproportionate commercial risk during development. Another drew a comparison with Silicon Valley’s tolerance for failure, arguing that Wales needs a similar cultural shift if it is to compete for capital on a global stage.

The cost pressures on smaller businesses were also raised directly, with corporation tax, national insurance and PAYE obligations cited as disincentives to growth. Attendees argued that fiscal incentives need to be rebalanced to make Wales a more competitive destination for founders and investors alike.

Skills and specialisation

On talent, the group’s clearest message was that the skills system in Wales should be employer-led rather than supply-driven. Several specific skills shortages were identified as part of an informal audit conducted during the discussion, though these were not published in detail. Attendees also cautioned against pursuing broad technology trends without first identifying the subsegments where Wales has a genuine comparative advantage, pointing to Admiral’s development of specialist insurance expertise as the model to follow.

Sarah Jones, chief executive of FinTech Wales, said the session produced clear actions: “One of the clearest messages from around the table was the need to create easier access to funding and remove some of the red tape that prevents companies being able to move swiftly in their respective markets.”

The minister closed the discussion by acknowledging Wales’ productivity gap relative to the rest of the UK and stressing the role of the recently established Welsh development agency in co-ordinating industry input. He committed the Welsh Government to continued engagement with the sector and to promoting Welsh fintech strengths internationally.

Broader context

Wales occupies a relatively modest position in the UK’s regional fintech landscape. While clusters in Cardiff have grown since FinTech Wales launched in 2019, the region competes with better-capitalised hubs in London, Edinburgh, Manchester and Leeds for both talent and venture funding. The UK government’s own regional investment policies, including Levelling Up commitments, have delivered mixed outcomes for financial services outside London, and Welsh Government devolved economic levers are limited compared with those available to the Scottish Government, which has its own fintech strategy and dedicated public funding vehicles.

The conversation at the FinTech Wales roundtable reflects a pattern visible across smaller regional ecosystems: structural barriers to capital and skills are well understood, but translating political engagement into concrete funding mechanisms or regulatory accommodations remains the harder step. The reference to a development agency open to industry input is worth monitoring, as is any follow-through on the sandbox proposal, which would require co-ordination with the FCA’s existing innovation pathways.

FinTech Wales has more than 200 members and operates as a not-for-profit body. Further details on its events programme are available at fintechwales.org.

title: FXB Summit 2026: why cross-border payments need partners
snippet: Instant payments, stablecoins and inclusion led the fourth FXB Summit in Dubai, where speakers agreed collaboration matters as much as the technology itself. The post FXB Summit 2026: why cross-border payments need partners appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The future of cross-border payments will depend as much on how financial institutions work together as on the technology they deploy. That was the message running through the fourth Future Cross Border (FXB) Payments Summit, held at the Anantara Downtown Dubai

The summit, founded by Shafique R Ibrahim and run by the events platform Fintership, brought banks, exchange houses, fintechs, payment providers and regulators together for a single day of panels and keynotes. Its supporting partners included the UAE Banks Federation, the Foreign Exchange and Remittance Group (FERG), Al Etihad Payments and Swift. The Fintech Times’ events correspondent Phil Smith was in attendance, and this summary draws on his notes from the day.

The agenda ranged across instant payments, artificial intelligence, digital assets, compliance and financial inclusion. In most sessions, the question was less whether the technology works and more how institutions, jurisdictions and regulators join it up.

A regulator that co-authors innovation

Adeeb Ahamed, Managing Director of LuLu Financial Holdings, credited the UAE’s supportive regulatory environment and its ability to attract international talent for the country’s rise as a financial innovation hub.

“The regulator has been a co-author for innovation here,” he said, pointing to the willingness of UAE authorities to back new business models.

His view of what comes next centred on partnership rather than building everything in-house. “I’m a great believer of partnerships. I believe that the future lies in partnerships,” he said. “Build what is necessary, and then find partners who can help you scale.”

On artificial intelligence, Ahamed described a human-in-the-loop approach at LuLu Financial Holdings. AI is being used to make areas such as compliance and auditing more efficient, while people retain oversight and customers keep control over their own financial decisions.

Taking instant payments across borders

Domestic instant payments have moved quickly in the UAE, where Al Etihad Payments operates the Aani instant payments platform. Carrying that speed across borders is a harder problem, and it was the focus of a panel with Andrea Cianchetti, Chief Product Officer at Al Etihad Payments, Roberto Mancone, CEO of du Pay, and Omer Farooq, CEO of Blue Remit.

Once a payment leaves the country, it meets foreign exchange conversion, settlement, differing regulatory requirements and the challenge of making separate systems interoperate. The panel’s view was that the domestic progress is real, but the international leg still carries most of the friction.

A separate session, Who Owns the Cross-Border Experience?, moderated by Muhammad Waqar Ashraf of Swift, asked who is accountable when a payment passes through several hands.

“The real challenge is moving value across institutions, jurisdictions and, of course, currencies,” said Nawal Kebouri Ammor, Group Head of Financial Institutions at Al Ansari Financial Services. She pointed to the differing settlement arrangements, liquidity requirements and regulatory frameworks that continue to complicate cross-border transactions.

Panellists also stressed that the experience of the person receiving a payment matters as much as that of the sender, particularly when the money moves through several financial institutions before it arrives.

Digital assets over the next 24 months

The practical use of digital assets was another focus, with speakers from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), RAKBANK, the Dubai Digital Asset Association and Fuze looking at what the next two years are likely to bring.

Stablecoins and tokenised money offer an alternative route for international settlement and money transfers. The panel was clear, however, that wider adoption will depend on regulatory clarity, liquidity and compatibility with the financial infrastructure banks already run. Speakers returned several times to the need for regulators, financial institutions and technology providers to work together as digital assets move into mainstream financial services, a point with particular weight in a city that set up a dedicated virtual assets regulator in 2022.

Financial inclusion beyond access

Syed Muhammad Ali, CEO of myZoi Financial Inclusion Technologies, focused on the lower-income workers who still rely heavily on cash, despite near-universal smartphone ownership in the UAE.

When myZoi began operating, more than 90 per cent of the salaries paid into its accounts were withdrawn in cash. Two years later, that figure had fallen below 50 per cent.

“The margin for error is non-existent,” Ali said. Many of these workers send a substantial share of their earnings home, so a single failed or delayed transfer can do lasting damage to trust. For this group, reliability is what drives digital adoption, not access alone.

Collaboration and competition

The summit also examined how the relationship between traditional institutions and technology-led providers is changing. Hasan Fardan Al Fardan, CEO of Al Fardan Exchange, took part in a leadership discussion on the roles each will play in cross-border payments, a theme he had set out ahead of the event: that progress depends on linking innovation with interoperability, governance and trust.

That framing carried through the wider discussion, as banks, exchange houses and fintechs described adapting to a payments landscape in which no single institution controls the full journey of a transaction.

By the close, the consistent challenge was turning technological progress into measurable improvements for consumers and businesses: international payments that are faster, cheaper, more transparent and more dependable. Those are the same four measures in the G20 roadmap for enhancing cross-border payments, coordinated by the Financial Stability Board, which sets its targets for cost, speed, transparency and access to be met by the end of 2027.

title: Interledger Foundation Maps Instant Payment Path for US CDFIs
snippet: The foundation's first domestic programme partners five community lenders to identify barriers blocking access to FedNow instant payment rails. The post Interledger Foundation Maps Instant Payment Path for US CDFIs appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The Interledger Foundation (ILF) has launched its first US-focused programme, partnering with five community development financial institutions (CDFIs) to identify the technical, regulatory and resource barriers that prevent community lenders from accessing instant payment infrastructure. The initiative, announced on 15 October 2026, marks a significant pivot for the San Francisco-based organisation, which has historically concentrated its interoperability work in Uganda, Mexico and across sub-Saharan Africa.

CDFIs collectively account for $272 billion in cumulative financing deployed to underserved communities in the United States. Despite that scale, most still operate on settlement rails that take days to clear, while large commercial banks have participated in real-time payment networks for years. The consequence is concrete: loan disbursements arrive late when borrowers need funds most urgently, and repayment friction pushes small business owners toward costlier alternatives.

The five projects

Chris Lawrence, chief programme officer at Interledger Foundation

The cohort spans diverse aspects of the payments gap. Village Micro Fund is investigating whether cooperative finance models, including community savings pools managed through its EnDAO platform, can connect to ACH, Fedwire and FedNow without requiring participants to hold or use cryptocurrency. Kiva is conducting listening sessions with Native entrepreneurs and Tribal communities to understand barriers to affordable capital before making any technology recommendation, a sequencing that resists the industry habit of deploying infrastructure ahead of community readiness.

Access to Capital for Entrepreneurs (ACE) is working in Georgia to feed real-time cash flow data into its borrower portal, with a longer-term objective of replacing historical credit averages with real-time cash flow as an underwriting input. Washington Area Community Investment Fund (WACIF) is researching how irregular cash flow patterns affect loan repayment behaviour, seeking to identify where flexible payment timing could reduce defaults among otherwise viable businesses. AltCap is building a post-closing payment modernisation roadmap for small business owners in the Kansas City region, grounded in direct borrower feedback.

“Community-based lenders have long operated on payment infrastructure that was never designed with them in mind,” said Chris Lawrence, chief programme officer at Interledger Foundation. “This initiative gives us the opportunity to understand precisely where those barriers are and ensure CDFIs are positioned to use the same instant payment rails that larger institutions have accessed for years.”

Regulatory tailwinds and sector context

The policy backdrop is relevant to how quickly this roadmap can translate into live infrastructure. The Federal Reserve’s proposed skinny master account, a limited-access account that would bundle direct FedNow and Fedwire connectivity, could give non-bank and smaller depository institutions a direct on-ramp to instant rails without the full compliance overhead of a standard master account. If the eligibility criteria broaden as proposed, CDFIs with the right charter status could connect directly rather than routing through a larger correspondent bank, reducing cost and latency.

The broader market context is one of uneven adoption. FedNow launched in July 2023 and has steadily added participating institutions, but uptake among smaller and mission-driven lenders has lagged behind the commercial banking sector. The ACE project’s ambition to build real-time cash flow underwriting sits alongside a growing cohort of open-banking and embedded-finance providers pursuing similar data-driven credit models, suggesting that the infrastructure gap ILF is mapping is one that commercial fintech has also identified as a market opportunity. The competitive question is whether CDFIs can access modernised rails on terms that preserve their mission economics, rather than being absorbed into commercial distribution networks.

ILF says the findings from the five projects will inform a broader roadmap for CDFI adoption of instant payment infrastructure. The current cohort is described as the first step in an ongoing initiative, with further partnerships expected.

title: Gr4vy and Unlimit Partner to Extend Local Payment Method Reach
snippet: The payment orchestration platform and global financial infrastructure firm will give enterprise merchants access to local methods across Latin America, Africa and Asia. The post Gr4vy and Unlimit Partner to Extend Local Payment Method Reach appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Gr4vy, the US-based cloud payment orchestration platform, has entered a partnership with Unlimit, the global financial infrastructure company, to extend the range of locally preferred payment methods available to Gr4vy’s enterprise merchant customers. The arrangement was announced on 8 October 2026 and takes effect through Gr4vy’s existing single integration layer.

The commercial logic is straightforward: enterprise merchants expanding internationally face a fragmented payment landscape in which consumer preferences, currencies and processing requirements vary sharply by market. Building a dedicated technical integration for each new market is costly and time-consuming. The partnership allows Gr4vy customers to access Unlimit’s acquiring and local payment network without modifying their existing stack.

The payment methods in scope

John Lunn, founder and chief executive of Gr4vy

The range of methods brought into scope through the deal is broad. In Latin America, merchants gain access to Pix and PicPay in Brazil, OXXO and Efectivo for cash-based markets in Mexico and elsewhere, and Mercado Pago’s wallet network. In Africa, the integration covers M-Pesa, the dominant mobile money rail across Kenya and several other sub-Saharan markets, alongside Airtel Money. In Asia-Pacific, WeChat Pay, GrabPay and UPI are included, addressing China, South-East Asia and India respectively. In Europe, MB WAY for Portugal and SEPA Instant round out the offering.

Irene Skrynova, CEO at Unlimit

John Lunn, founder and chief executive of Gr4vy, said the partnership gives customers “the flexibility to add the local payment methods they need as they expand internationally, without rebuilding their financial stack.” Irene Skrynova, chief executive of global payments at Unlimit, characterised payments as “fundamentally local,” citing customer preferences, currencies and processing requirements as sources of complexity for internationally expanding businesses.

Market context and competitive positioning

Payment orchestration has matured rapidly as a category. Platforms such as Gr4vy compete in a segment that now includes several well-funded European and US-based rivals, with the core proposition being a single integration that routes transactions across multiple payment service providers and methods. The competitive differentiator has increasingly shifted from the orchestration layer itself, which is becoming commoditised, to the depth and geographic spread of the underlying payment method coverage.

On that metric, the Unlimit partnership adds meaningful weight. Unlimit’s own network reportedly spans more than 180 countries and holds licences in 97 jurisdictions, making it one of the more geographically extensive independent payment networks available. The inclusion of Pix is particularly notable: Brazil’s central bank-operated instant payment scheme processed more than 60 billion transactions in 2024 and has become a prerequisite for any serious Latin America e-commerce play.

Regulatory read-across is relevant here too. UPI cross-border expansion is subject to agreements between the National Payments Corporation of India and host-country regulators, while SEPA Instant is entering a mandatory phase for eurozone payment service providers under the EU’s updated instant payments regulation, meaning demand from European-facing merchants is likely to grow regardless of competitive pressures. For Gr4vy, anchoring local-method access to a licensed counterparty such as Unlimit reduces the direct regulatory burden on the orchestration layer itself.

The partnership does not include disclosed commercial terms, transaction volume targets or named launch customers beyond those listed in Unlimit’s existing client roster, which includes Xiaomi, Telegram and Convera. The near-term test is whether the combined offering accelerates merchant onboarding into markets such as Brazil and India, where local payment method adoption has historically been the primary friction point for international entrants.

title: AI’s real opportunity in payments is giving experts back their time
snippet: Advancing operational efficiency through intelligent guidance on errors and exception handling.
fullText:
Sponsored content

        
    
    
        

SPONSORED CONTENT BY
            
        

    

Picture a payments operator working through an exception queue. An item kicks out, and before it can be fixed, someone has to determine why: pull the transaction data, trace it through the relevant systems, check it against the rules of the network it is moving through and then decide on a corrective action. That kind of process plays out again and again across a bank's payment operations, every day, many times a day. Payment processing errors and exception handling remain both a heavy manual burden on operations teams and a detractor for overall end-customer experience, with disruptions costing the industry billions of dollars every year.

As payment volumes continue to rise, there is a big opportunity for banks to address this persistent pain point in payment operations and fuel growth. AI-driven automation that maintains human oversight offers a promising way to reimagine inefficient payment error and exception-handling processes by accelerating repairs, streamlining onboarding and improving the overall customer experience.

Accelerating repairs

Now consider that same operator working from a different starting point. AI has already surfaced the likely cause of the discrepancy, checked it against the applicable payment rules and recommended a fix. The operator reviews an assembled case, corrects it where needed and approves it, rather than building it from scratch. That is a faster task. Finastra’s data shows that this kind of guidance can reduce manual investigation time by 20-30%, saving payment operations teams more than 1.5 hours a day that would otherwise be spent diagnosing the same category of problem without this capability. That speed creates real operational capacity, enabling teams to handle more high-value customer experiences and create differentiation.

Enhancing operator onboarding

Payments infrastructure at most financial institutions is complex, built on years of integrations with institutional knowledge often concentrated among a handful of experienced staff. This makes learning a bank's payment systems no small task and places a premium on specialized skillsets. AI-powered automation capabilities targeted to support payment error reconciliation can shorten the learning curve by acting as a guide, helping new hires navigate the system and find the documentation or precedent they need. Just as important, it augments the specialized human expertise within organizations, since reliable repair guidance is now built into the workflow.

Becoming resilient and future proof

Payment rails are not static. Real-time schemes continue to roll out, ISO 20022 migration is reshaping message standards across markets, and cross-border corridors carry their own compliance requirements. A recommendation that is not validated against the current rules of the network a payment is moving through, such as SWIFT, Fedwire, SEPA, UPI or Nexus, cannot be trusted. Scheme-aware repair recommendations should identify discrepancies and underlying causes, delivering a proposed fix that is accurate and compliant with scheme and network requirements. With cloud-native infrastructure, AI-powered payments reconciliation recommender capabilities provide the flexibility to update rules without multi-year re-platforming whenever a standard changes. That combination is what resilience means in payment operations: staying accurate and compliant as the rules governing payments continue to change.

Modernization and AI readiness are becoming less of an efficiency upgrade and more of a growth requirement. The time, manual effort and specialized expertise required to keep error and exception-handling operations running smoothly have, for years, limited how quickly banks can scale. Solving that back-office barrier is part of what will separate the institutions that grow from those that do not.

fullText:
Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

title: Money20/20 USA preview: Las Vegas opens with trust as the price of every new rail
snippet: The Fintech Times is on the ground this week, filing a daily round-up and recording conversations on the floor. The post Money20/20 USA preview: Las Vegas opens with trust as the price of every new rail appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
The Money Hall opens on Monday at The Venetian with more than 630 speakers and four days of programme. After Riyadh and Miami, The Fintech Times expects the same argument in a louder room, which is who carries the risk when stablecoins, tokenised deposits and AI agents move money for real.

Money20/20 USA opens its exhibition floor on Monday morning at The Venetian in Las Vegas, the day after a Sunday of summits and the Money Awards, and runs to midday on Wednesday. The organiser expects more than 11,000 people from 3,400 companies, with 630-plus speakers and 180 exhibitors appearing for the first time, and has built the programme around four pillars: borderless financial architecture, technology as the great equaliser, partnerships as the engine to scale, and a brave new world of guardrails.

The Fintech Times is on the ground this week, filing a daily round-up and recording conversations on the floor. If you are in Las Vegas and have something worth saying, the editorial desk is at [email protected].

The argument we brought with us

This is the third big fintech gathering we have covered in five weeks, and the three are starting to read as one conversation. In Riyadh in September the market-opening decisions came from the regulator rather than the companies, with SAMA enabling Alipay+ and setting out Tap to Pay on iPhone while the industry got on with building. In Miami two weeks later Sibos spent four days agreeing that the technology for tokenised money and AI agents is no longer the question; the question is who carries the trust when it goes wrong.

Las Vegas is where the United States gives its answer, and the organiser knows it. Jessica Blue, who runs the show, put the practical questions plainly in the run-up: who holds the value, who verifies identity, who settles the transaction and who is responsible when something goes wrong. That is exactly the list Miami left open.

Monday: the bank, then the money

Bill Demchak, Chairman and Chief Executive of PNC, takes the Exchange Stage at 10:00 to talk about the next era of banking, and he is followed almost immediately by the session we would not miss, a 10:20 debate on whether tokenised bank deposits and stablecoins are complementary or competitive. At Sibos the banks had largely decided that question in favour of deposits, because they are bank money on bank rails under bank regulation, with stablecoins doing the weekend and exotic-corridor work banks cannot. Las Vegas is a stablecoin-native crowd and will push back.

The regulatory backdrop makes this a strange year to pitch a stablecoin product. The GENIUS Act’s deadline for final rules passed in July without them; the Comptroller said last week that the OCC’s rule should land before the end of October, and the Treasury’s own comment period on issuance closes today. Everyone demonstrating a dollar coin in the hall is building against rules that could still move. Mastercard and BVNK take that on directly at 11:15 with a session on stablecoin security and trust, and Visa arrives having moved Visa Direct’s stablecoin-funded prefunding from pilot to production last week, with USDC now settling cross-border payouts in near real time for its first enabler.

The demand side is more cautious than the stage will suggest. Research from the cross-border fintech Neo, shared with us ahead of the show, found that 88 per cent of finance leaders at internationally trading SMEs think stablecoins could improve their collections, and 27 per cent accept them. That gap is the real state of the market.

Agents: from capability to accountability

The loudest word on the floor will be agentic, and the useful sessions will be the ones that ask about liability rather than capability. Mastercard’s Trust Layer for Agentic Commerce at 14:10, with Skyfire and Forter, is built on the premise that a payments network needs to understand the context and risk behind every agent-initiated interaction, which is the industry’s polite way of saying it does not yet. Sunday’s cybersecurity summit opened with a panel titled Who Let the Bots Pay, and the phrase Know Your Agent will follow you around the hall all week.

The identity companies are treating this as their moment. World used Sunday to launch a World ID suite for banking and finance, including a credential for agents, and Proof’s x401, launched last week, lets a website check who is behind an agent and exactly what that person approved before it acts. The problem both are solving showed up in a readiness index published last week, which sent an AI agent to more than a thousand organisations and found that none of the 18 banks tested could talk to it, and several block declared agents outright.

Consumers are not rushing them either: an August survey of 1,000 US adults found 11 per cent had let an agent complete a purchase and 69 per cent did not trust one to pay securely. In Miami the practical bankers told us the sensible order is agents repairing payments first and paying later, with a mandate underneath. Watch whether anyone in Las Vegas says the same.

The customer, the rails and the regulator

Two Monday items speak to the person at the end of all this. Mastercard’s Sherri Haymond argues at 12:05 that the only branch you will ever need is a wallet, and Huntington Bank is announcing a small business operating system built with Google Cloud that puts agentic tools in front of owners rather than engineers. Later in the week Cameron Fowler of Early Warning, which operates Zelle, keynotes on the real-time rails the banks still own and the ones they are adopting that they do not, and on Tuesday FDIC Chairman Travis Hill sits down with the Financial Technology Association, the most consequential regulator slot of the show.

Monday closes on the Intersection Stage at 15:55 with former CFTC Chairman J. Christopher Giancarlo asking whether policy serves everyday users or mainly institutions. Riyadh said the regulator opens the door. Miami said the bank is the gatekeeper of trust. Las Vegas has to say who pays when the agent gets it wrong.

The Money Hall opens at 09:00 Pacific time. Our day one round-up follows on Monday evening.

title: MorganAsh Adds BSL Translation via Signly to Meet Consumer Duty
snippet: MorganAsh has partnered with Signly to offer human BSL translations across its sites, citing Consumer Duty accessibility obligations for the UK's deaf community. The post MorganAsh Adds BSL Translation via Signly to Meet Consumer Duty appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
MorganAsh, a specialist in Consumer Duty compliance and customer vulnerability, has integrated British Sign Language translation technology from Signly across its main website and its consumer portal, itswhoiam.me. The move makes MorganAsh one of a growing number of financial services firms deploying on-demand BSL translation to satisfy accessibility requirements under the FCA‘s Consumer Duty rules.

Signly’s service works by connecting organisations with registered BSL translators, all of whom are members of the deaf community. Visitors to either site can request a translation of any webpage at no cost. Once a translation is produced, it is stored and updated automatically whenever the underlying content changes. The company is explicit that its translations are produced by human professionals rather than AI-generated sign language, a distinction that matters for quality and community trust.

Consumer Duty context

Andrew Gething, managing director of MorganAsh

Consumer Duty, which came into full effect for open products in July 2023 and for closed books in July 2024, places a positive obligation on firms to ensure customers can access, understand and act on information in a way that leads to good outcomes. The FCA has been clear that accessibility for vulnerable customers is central to that obligation, not a secondary consideration.

Andrew Gething, managing director of MorganAsh, said: “If a person cannot access important financial information in a format that works for them, they risk being excluded from making informed decisions. It’s therefore not just about good practice, but about delivering good outcomes and creating a financial services sector that is fairer, more trusted and more inclusive for everyone.”

The release notes that roughly 87,000 people in the UK use BSL as their primary language, with a broader estimate of around 151,000 people using BSL in some form. A point MorganAsh and Signly both emphasise is that profound deafness does not automatically confer English literacy: for a significant portion of the deaf community, BSL is a first language, and written English is, in effect, a second. Financial services websites that assume text accessibility is sufficient may still be falling short of their Consumer Duty obligations.

Signly already counts Lloyds Bank, Santander and Nationwide among its financial services clients, which gives MorganAsh a degree of third-party validation for the technology before it integrates it into its own vulnerability-management tooling.

Market positioning

The partnership is also commercially rational for MorganAsh. The firm’s flagship product, the MorganAsh Resilience System (MARS), is positioned as a tool that helps financial services providers identify and monitor vulnerable customers and generate a standardised Resilience Rating. Embedding BSL accessibility directly into itswhoiam.me, the consumer-facing portal designed to help customers disclose vulnerabilities to firms, strengthens the coherence of that product proposition. A portal asking customers to self-report vulnerability must itself be fully accessible to those it seeks to serve.

More broadly, the FCA has indicated that it will scrutinise how firms evidence their Consumer Duty compliance, with vulnerability management and accessibility among the areas it is most likely to probe in supervisory review cycles. Firms that have not audited their digital estate for sign-language accessibility may find this partnership a useful prompt to do so. Signly’s automated workflow also means that ongoing maintenance burden for participating firms is relatively low once initial translation work is done.

The next milestones to watch are whether adoption among smaller financial services firms accelerates following high-street bank deployments, and whether the FCA issues more prescriptive guidance on digital accessibility standards under Consumer Duty in the coming review period.

title: Standard Chartered VCC Platform Hits $2.6bn AUM with 10th Sub-Fund
snippet: Standard Chartered has launched its tenth VCC sub-fund with BNY Investments, a cash management vehicle targeting accredited investors across six markets. The post Standard Chartered VCC Platform Hits $2.6bn AUM with 10th Sub-Fund appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Standard Chartered has crossed $2.6 billion in assets under management on its Variable Capital Company platform, marking the milestone alongside the launch of a tenth sub-fund in partnership with BNY Investments. The Signature Select Premium Cash Reserve Fund is an enhanced cash management product managed by Insight Investment, the fixed income arm of BNY Investments, and will be made available to Accredited and Professional Investor clients across Priority, Priority Private and Private Banking segments in Hong Kong, Singapore, the UAE, Jersey, Kenya and Nigeria.

The fund targets returns above the Secured Overnight Financing Rate by investing in a diversified portfolio of high-quality short-term fixed income and money market instruments, with daily liquidity. It is the bank’s fifth VCC sub-fund launch in 2026 and comes roughly two years after the platform was established in June 2024.

The deal

Ayesha Abbas, managing director and head of affluent and wealth solutions for EMEA and the UAE at Standard Chartered

Sumeet Bhambri, global head of advisory and managed investments at Standard Chartered, noted that the $2.6 billion figure reflects “strong momentum” since inception and framed the bank’s approach as delivering institutionally managed strategies through partnerships with external asset managers rather than building proprietary funds. The VCC structure, established under Singapore’s regulatory framework, allows for multiple sub-funds under a single corporate umbrella, reducing administrative overhead and enabling faster fund launches.

Ayesha Abbas, managing director and head of affluent and wealth solutions for EMEA and the UAE at Standard Chartered, pointed to client demand for capital preservation alongside above-cash returns, citing “evolving market conditions” as the driver. Doni Shamsuddin, head of Asia Pacific at BNY Investments, said cash was playing an increasingly important role in portfolio construction as investors sought resilience and flexibility.

The UAE sits at the centre of Standard Chartered’s regional pitch. The bank describes the country as a wealth hub benefiting from inflows of global talent and internationally mobile entrepreneurs, a characterisation that aligns with a broader competition among private banks and asset managers to capture a growing pool of high-net-worth capital in the Gulf.

Market context

The enhanced cash management category has attracted significant institutional attention since interest rates rose sharply from 2022 onwards. With central banks in several major economies beginning to ease, investors are now weighing whether to lock into longer-duration fixed income or maintain the optionality of short-duration, liquid instruments. A SOFR-linked, daily-liquidity product sits squarely in the second camp and is positioned as a holding vehicle rather than a long-term allocation.

Standard Chartered is not alone in pursuing this segment through a fund platform architecture. Several international private banks and wealth managers have used the Singapore VCC framework, introduced in 2020, to consolidate product manufacturing and reduce fund formation costs. The VCC’s pass-through tax treatment and flexible redemption rules make it an efficient vehicle for rolling out differentiated strategies to accredited clients across Asia, the Middle East and Africa, the geographies where Standard Chartered has its deepest retail wealth franchise.

The bank’s partnership model, where it distributes funds managed by external specialists such as Insight Investment rather than running its own in-house investment teams, mirrors an asset-light approach common among distribution-led wealth platforms. The key commercial risk in that model is that the bank’s differentiation rests on curation and client access rather than investment alpha, which puts pressure on fund selection discipline and manager due diligence over time.

The next markers to watch are whether the platform reaches its next AUM threshold before the end of 2026 and which additional markets are added to the fund’s distribution list.

title: Utah forms digital ID consortium
snippet: The state is using its digital identity law as a model for having individuals, not governments, control their personal data, Utah’s chief privacy officer said.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The state is using its digital identity law as a model for having individuals, not governments, control their personal data, Utah’s chief privacy officer said.

        

            

        Published Oct. 19, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                States are working together to craft regulations related to digital identities. It's an important issue in payments because personal data is tied to transactions.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Utah is forming a multi-state consortium of governors to advance a governance framework and principles for state-issued digital identification credentials, Utah’s chief privacy officer said Sunday on the first day of the Money20/20 financial technology conference. The coalition is focused on advancing the idea that people inherently own their identification data and should be able to limit how much personal information they share through their digital IDs.

Utah hasn’t announced which states have joined the group, and is awaiting “a few more that will be aligning around these shared principles,” Christopher Bramwell, Utah’s chief privacy officer, said at the discussion on digital identification. By January, 10 states will have either their legislatures or executive branches working on ID governance frameworks modeled after Utah’s privacy-focused “state-endorsed digital identity" program, he said.

States such as Utah and California have been leading in the area of digital identity, said Jennifer Kerber, head of global government affairs for Socure, a digital ID verification and fraud-prevention firm, who spoke with Bramwell during the Sunday panel. California has about 2.2 million digital IDs in use, she said.

Dive Insight:

Digital identities raise important issues in the payments realm because such personal information is often tied to transactions, particularly in e-commerce. That's becoming an increasingly key issue as more fintechs aim to use that data to personalize services.

Currently, 21 states and Puerto Rico issue digital IDs, according to the Transportation Security Administration. 

Utah enacted what it called the first digital ID “bill of rights” law earlier this year, which created a “state-endorsed digital identity” program aimed at giving people control of their identity data.

“What good is digital identity if nothing in it says that somebody can't use it to do surveillance pricing in a way that harms you, or they can't track and surveil every single usage of it?” said Bramwell, who is also director of the Utah Office of Data Privacy.

States need a governance framework for IDs because there are “168 million different digital identities in use across different platforms in the U.S. lacking these rules of the road,” he said.

Ajay Gupta, chief digital transformation officer for the California Department of Motor Vehicles, was also scheduled to appear at the panel. Ultimately, he didn’t appear, with Kerber pointing to travel complications.

Utah is working toward an ID system that would render a person’s data, if it’s breached, virtually useless for fraud and impersonation, because the criminal doesn’t have access to the ID credentials, he said. “How do we empower each of you to have something you control, so that even when your personal data has been breached, it can't be used to impersonate you and commit fraud?” he said. 

Utah began its digital ID work by establishing a policy framework before issuing any products, Bramwell said. With the policy framework passed, Utah officials have begun working on the technology to power the new IDs. “Now we're working on the tech to actually come in and say, ‘What are we actually able to do?’” Bramwell said.

The range of digital IDs across states so far has provided Utah insights on various approaches, he said. 

Utah hopes that as it works with other states, “we actually end up meeting in the middle where we bring the governance, they brought some of the tech, and we'll all be able to exist in this ecosystem, regardless of which technology approach,” Bramwell said.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

fullText:
Speech by Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges, at the Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026.

  

Speaker: Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges 

Event: Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026

Delivered: 5 October 2026  

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 9 minutes

Highlights:

The FCA’s wide-ranging reforms over recent years are making UK capital markets more effective, competitive and attractive.

Trust, market integrity and high standards set the foundations for sustainable growth, and it is crucial that we also enable informed risk-taking.

We’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets by supporting innovation, including tokenisation.

    

            						

The Economic Secretary to the Treasury has discussed the contribution of UK markets to economic growth. 

I want to build on that by talking about the FCA’s role in reforming capital market rules.

The headline is that we've been very busy over the past few years. 

We’ve now completed major aspects of a multi-year programme of work, to ensure capital markets work well for our economy and support growth.

This has already delivered positive changes. But there’s plenty more to come.

We are working on further reforms, while also adapting to rapid changes in markets and use of technology.

In fact, areas such as tokenisation, AI and markets for trading private company shares have become central to our capital markets policy programme. 

And that tells us something important. As markets change, our approach has had to change too.

The question has not been whether regulation changes. It has been how we adjust in a way that preserves trust while also supporting innovation and growth.

Let me start by talking about our approach to the work.

We have been working with the Treasury, the Bank of England and in close dialogue with the private sector, on a raft of wholesale market reforms.

These draw on formal reports, like the Wholesale Markets Review, our process of reviewing inherited EU regulation, and issues raised by market contacts.

Some have suggested the work programme is a list not a strategy. But I think that underestimates it. There are some key principles running through it.

          

            						

Reforming from a position of strength

First, we are reforming from a position of strength, by building on the UK’s advantages.

The UK is home to deep, trusted and internationally connected capital markets. 

London continues to rank among the world’s leading financial centres. Our markets are respected and characterised by strong institutions and a reputation for integrity.

And the UK offers a full range of markets and services, supported by a diverse system of issuers, investors, intermediaries and infrastructure.

So our work programme is broad too. Covering primary markets, secondary markets, post-trade arrangements and a broad range of assets.

But successful markets cannot stand still.

Capital is increasingly mobile. Technology is reshaping markets. Private markets have grown. And new forms of trading and market infrastructure are emerging.

So our challenge is to preserve these strengths, whilst keeping UK markets dynamic and internationally competitive.

          

            						

Rebalancing risk

In some areas this requires us to think differently about regulation.

For a while, financial regulation became more detailed and prescriptive. Often for understandable reasons following periods of market stress.

But we know that growth, innovation and investment all depend on taking risk.

That is why our approach is founded on the principle of maintaining high standards while creating more space for informed risk-taking and innovation. 

This is especially relevant in wholesale markets, where professional participants assess opportunities and weigh risks every day.

Our role is to create regulation that enables this through clear rules and good disclosures, so that firms and investors can make informed decisions.

This is what we mean when we talk about rebalancing risk.

It does not mean lowering standards or weakening market integrity.

It means being deliberate about where regulation is needed and where market participants can take decisions themselves, armed with good information and appropriate disclosures.

In many cases, that means we can shift away from detailed prescription towards outcomes, transparency and accountability.

In doing so, we must never forget the underlying objective.

Ultimately, we want companies to have good options for how to raise capital, so they can invest and grow. And investors to have access to a broad range of investment opportunities.

Regulation cannot, on its own, drive economic growth. But good regulation and markets that work well are vital for a healthy economy.

          

            						

Turning reform into results

You can see our approach in the reforms we have already delivered.

We have completed around 30 capital-markets focused workstreams. And there’s an even larger number across the FCA’s broader work.

That’s too many to discuss individually in this speech. There’s a list below, but to summarise some of them:

In primary markets, we introduced once-in-a-generation changes to the UK listing regime, significantly reducing costs for issuers and supporting competitiveness with other jurisdictions. Since then, we have seen many corporate transactions that have been simplified as a result. And around 25 companies have joined the Main Market, including 7 IPOs in H1 2026.

Our new public offers framework raised the thresholds for when prospectuses are needed by companies raising capital and we also introduced public offer platforms to facilitate off-market fundraising. We have already seen a rise in capital raised by companies, including via debt markets, alongside the broader benefits of a simpler and more flexible regime.

In secondary markets, we have significantly improved transparency in bond and derivatives markets. This includes the bond consolidated tape, which launched in June – the first consolidated tape outside North America – which already has 1.6 million licences subscribed to it. These changes are shining a new light on UK markets, delivering a 70% increase in corporate bond trades and 30% for government bond trades observed in real time and enhancing the way market participants view the market.

We are moving towards an equity consolidated tape too and will appoint a provider next year. In the meantime, we launched a market activity report, so investors see the true scale of UK equity trading.

We have also responded to the growth of private markets through the creation of PISCES, a new market for trading in private company shares. Four operators have been authorised and we’ve seen seven transactions – involving companies ranging from tech firms, to brewers and board-game makers.

In post-trade, we’ve adjusted transaction reporting, with initial proposals estimated to save firms £100m per year.

And we’ve altered some of the clearing and margining rules, including increasing the clearing threshold for commodity derivatives following volatility in commodity markets.

On the investor side, we are streamlining regulatory requirements for the asset management sector, via the AIFMD review, and supporting the government in its review of the pension market.

We’re also supporting retail participation by improving access to investment advice and simplifying product information.

And our changes to primary market rules have positively impacted retail investment. We’ve seen a 50% increase in the value of retail-denominated corporate bonds and an increase in domestic retail investor allocation in fundraisings.

We are not done though.

A range of further reforms are planned or underway.

For example, on securitisation markets; listed company disclosures; benchmarks; and rules on clearing and margining.

We’re always in listening mode. So if you have ideas that would benefit UK markets please tell us.

          

            						

Competitiveness without compromise

We are doing this work to make markets work better, which is our statutory objective.

By doing that, we support growth and international competitiveness.

Capital is mobile. Businesses have choices about where they raise finance, invest and operate. The UK cannot ignore that reality.

But competitiveness does not come from a race to the bottom.

The UK's reputation for openness, stability and high standards is a strategic asset.

Our approach is pragmatic. We will challenge inherited rules when they no longer serve markets effectively, learn from other jurisdictions, and recognise the value of international consistency.

But we will do so without compromising market integrity, which provides the bedrock for sustainable growth.

          

            						

Preparing for tomorrow’s markets

I want to finish by talking about how we’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets.

We want to support innovation. To ensure markets evolve and use technology that opens up opportunities, efficiencies and encourages new entrants.

One example is working with firms to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI. Through our AI Lab, the AI Consortium with the Bank, and innovation sandboxes that allow firms to test ideas with us. 

And we are enabling firms and markets to explore tokenisation.

With the Bank and Treasury, we set up the Digital Securities Sandbox, which will support issuance of the new digital gilt (or DIGIT) early next year. Many think that the success of DIGIT can catalyse digital activity in UK.

We have worked with industry on new rules and governance for tokenised investment funds and the launch of the UK’s first fully-native tokenised fund.

And with Treasury and the Bank we’ve developed a regulatory framework for stablecoins.

But we are at a critical point. Keeping pace with other jurisdictions will require effective coordination between the private and public sectors. Industry leadership will be at least as important as public policy. 

Firms need to build, scale and innovate, moving beyond pilots to demonstrate real commercial use.

The UK’s Wholesale Digital Markets Champion, Chris Woolard, is playing a key role in coordinating the sector.

We know that regulatory clarity matters too. That’s why in May we published a joint vision with the Bank of England, setting out the regulatory principles for tokenised wholesale markets.

The feedback was clear. Industry wants to move quickly. In turn, we will provide certainty in areas such as prudential treatment, custody and market infrastructure.

We share the sense of urgency.

In coming weeks we will publish a joint roadmap, setting out how the UK’s wholesale markets will adapt as we work collectively to realise the benefits from tokenisation and digitalization.

Our objective is not to predict exactly what future markets will look like.

It is to ensure that our regulatory framework can adapt as markets evolve.

          

            						

Conclusion

We want UK capital markets to remain among the most trusted in the world, whilst also being among the most innovative, competitive and attractive. Markets that allow businesses to raise capital, help investors, and support the wider economy.

Our wide-ranging reforms have already delivered positive outcomes, across a variety of markets.

The approach is to build on the UK’s strengths and enable informed risk-taking, while preserving the trust, integrity and high standards on which successful markets depend.

The programme of reform will continue to evolve as markets change.

But the direction is clear. We are building markets that are ready not only for today's economy but for tomorrow's as well.

          

        

Capital market reforms completed in recent years

      						Post-trade, investors and cross-cutting

Three new appointments have been made to our Board, bringing additional experience in public policy, financial services, regulation and corporate leadership as we continue to deliver our strategy.

snippet: Mox Bank has launched Home Cushion Insurance in Hong Kong, a QBE-underwritten policy covering contents, buildings, liability and pets in a single digital product. The post Mox Bank Adds Home Insurance to its Mox Insure Digital Suite appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Mox Bank has launched Home Cushion Insurance, a fully digital home insurance product available through the Mox app and underwritten by QBE Hongkong and Shanghai Insurance Limited. The product is available to renters, owner-occupiers and landlords in Hong Kong and consolidates building structures, home contents and third-party liability into a single policy, alongside optional cover for pet accommodation and relocation costs.

The policy is offered across three tiers (Basic, Value and Max) and provides up to HKD 1,500,000 in home contents cover and HKD 100,000 for buildings, with third-party liability of up to HKD 10,000,000. A notable feature is its replacement-as-new settlement approach, under which eligible claims on home contents are settled at full replacement cost without depreciation applied. Relocation cover extends protection simultaneously to an existing and a new home for up to 28 days, plus transit cover of up to 15 per cent of the sum insured.

The Mox Insure build-out

Philip Wong, chief commercial officer at Mox Bank

Home Cushion Insurance is the fourth insurance product launched under the Mox Insure banner and the third distinct product line, following Personal Accident Cushion and Travel Pick and Go. The pace of expansion, four products with QBE in roughly 12 months, reflects a deliberate strategy to extend Mox beyond core banking into wealth protection, a segment that digital banks globally have found difficult to monetise at scale. Mox acts as a licensed insurance agent (licence number GA1073) rather than the insurer itself, distributing under an exclusive agreement with QBE Hong Kong.

Philip Wong, chief commercial officer of Mox, said the bank’s customers expect managing and protecting their wealth to be “seamless, intuitive, and entirely digital”, adding that insurance should meet the same standard. Lei Yu, CEO of QBE North Asia, noted the home product was the fourth collaboration with Mox in their first year of partnership.

Market context

Hong Kong’s insurtech and embedded-finance landscape is competitive. Several digital banking licensees, including ZA Bank and WeLab Bank, have moved into insurance distribution as a way to deepen customer relationships and generate fee income beyond lending and deposits. The bancassurance model is well established in Hong Kong through traditional retail banks, meaning Mox and its virtual-bank peers are competing against entrenched distribution networks with long-standing insurer relationships.

The embedded insurance angle is where digital banks may hold a structural advantage: frictionless in-app enrolment, pre-filled customer data and no paper forms reduce drop-off at the point of sale. Whether that translates into meaningfully higher attach rates than branch-based or broker-led distribution is still an open question across the sector.

From a regulatory standpoint, Hong Kong’s Insurance Authority has been an active licensor of both insurers and insurance agents operating through digital channels. The IA Levy framework, which applies to all eligible policies, adds a small cost layer that Mox flags in its product documentation. The Financial Dispute Resolution Scheme applies to selling-process disputes, while contractual disputes are handled directly between the policyholder and QBE, a split that is standard for agent-distributed products but worth noting for customers unfamiliar with that structure.

Mox, which is backed by Standard Chartered, PCCW, HKT and Trip.com, launched in September 2020 and holds the seventh-largest credit card portfolio among Hong Kong retail banks by portfolio size, according to TransUnion data for the first half of 2026. The bank’s technology stack has also been transferred to Trust Bank in Singapore, suggesting a degree of regional export ambition beyond the insurance product itself.

title: The 67% signal: Why card issuers should act on flexible credentials
snippet: 67% want one card for debit, credit and BNPL. Don’t let a competitor give it to them first.
fullText:
Marqeta’s 2026 State of Credit Report found that 67% of consumers would replace their primary debit card with a flexible credential. This isn’t curiosity but preference, and the gap between what consumers want and what most card programs offer is widening fast.

What’s a flexible credential?

A single payment card that adapts to context. At checkout, the cardholder can pay with debit, draw on a credit line, split the purchase into BNPL installments, or combine funding sources. The form factor stays the same while the payment method changes. These products are live in market today, so the question for issuers is whether they’re positioned to deliver one.

Why consumers want them

Interest is strongest among younger consumers: 48% of 18 to 44 year olds are interested, and 60% of 18 to 34 year olds started their financial journey with a credit product, which makes them more attuned to flexibility. Consumers say they want to:

Use the right payment method for each purchase without carrying multiple cards

Access BNPL for larger purchases without opening a separate account

Manage cash flow at the point of sale, not after the fact

Avoid managing multiple provider relationships

Notably, 71% of consumers with multiple credit cards want to switch between credit products at checkout. They already have the products but can’t use them fluidly in one transaction.

The cost of not delivering

Consumers switch providers because of improved credit scores, life changes, or better rewards elsewhere, not because something went wrong. Providers won’t lose customers in a dramatic moment. They’ll lose them gradually, one contextual payment decision at a time, as customers reach for a different card when theirs can’t do what’s needed. With flexible credentials increasingly visible on social feeds, through peers, and at checkout, that moment is coming soon. With a flexible credential, the relationship deepens rather than fragments.

Marqeta platform data shows the shift is underway: through the first five months of 2025, BNPL average order values fell 9% year over year, while non-discretionary spend TPV rose more than 60% from 2023 to 2024. Consumers are folding BNPL into everyday spending.

The SMB opportunity

60% of SMBs are interested in flexible payment orchestration, with interest rising among growth-stage businesses. A single card that can pay a supplier on net terms, split an equipment purchase into installments, and draw on credit for operating expenses offers something no static card can. SMBs represent one of the largest untapped opportunities in credit today.

What issuers need to get right

The question isn’t whether to offer flexible credentials but when, and on what infrastructure. Providers that move now will win customers actively looking for this product, while those that wait will find them locked in with faster competitors.

Infrastructure: A platform that handles multiple payment types, real-time decisioning, and dynamic credential switching through a single API. Stitching together separate debit, credit, and BNPL point solutions won’t deliver the seamless experience consumers expect.

The credit product underneath: Programmable credit infrastructure that lets program managers set their own approval models, limits, and terms.

The consumer experience: Switching at checkout must be effortless, or the experience fails regardless of the infrastructure.

The bottom line

When 67% of consumers say they’d replace their primary debit card, they’re describing a product they’d adopt from a provider they already trust. Those who respond with the right product on the right infrastructure will hold a durable advantage in consumer and SMB credit for the next decade.
